e-6629.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
e-6629.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 4y = 0,\quad x > 0.
$$
e-6629.worked_solution:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form $y=x^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda x^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)x^{\lambda-2}
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+4{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +4] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda  & =\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(x)=c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{x} )  + c_2\sin( 2 \ln{x} ).
$$

e-6630.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
e-6630.problem:
Determine the general solution to the equation

$$
t^2 y'' +5ty'+8y = 0,\quad t\gt 0.
$$
e-6630.worked_solution:
This is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume the solutions take the form $y=t^\lambda.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
y' = \lambda t^{\lambda -1}, \qquad y'' = \lambda(\lambda-1)t^{\lambda-2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+5t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+8{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +8] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +8 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +8 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+8 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
y(t) = t^{-2} \left( c_1 \cos( 2 \ln{t} ) + c_2 \sin( 2 \ln{t} ) \right).
$$

e-6631.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
e-6631.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 49 y = 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)= c_1 \cos(7 \ln{x} )  + c_2\sin(7 \ln{x} ),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
x^2 y'' + xy' + 49 y = 0, \quad y(1) = 0, \quad y'(1) = -7, \quad x > 0.
$$
e-6631.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1) = 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0 = c_1.
$$

- To apply the condition $y'(1) = -7,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\frac{7}{x}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(1) = -7$ and $c_1 = 0$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =7{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x) = -\sin(7 \ln{x} ).
$$

e-6632.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
e-6632.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
2t^2 y'' -2ty' +20 y= 0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y = t(c_1 \cos( 3 \ln{t} ) + c_2\sin( 3 \ln{t}) ),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
2t^2 y'' -2ty' +20 y= 0, \quad y(1)= 0,  \quad y'(1) = -1, \quad t\gt 0.
$$
e-6632.worked_solution:
We find the constants $c_1$ and $c_2$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1) = 0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0  = c_1.
$$

- To apply the condition $y'(1) = -1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={c}_{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y'(1) = -1$ and $c_1=0$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =3{c}_{2} \\ -\frac{1}{3} & ={c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t) = -\dfrac{ t\sin( 3 \ln{t}) )}{3}.
$$

Question 1
?

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+xy′+16y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡4x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡4x)
b
y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡2x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡2x)
c
y(x)=c1x+c24xln⁡x
d
y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=c14x2+c24x2
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^λ gives λ(λ−1)+λ+16=λ²+16=0, so λ=±4i. Thus the general solution is c₁cos(4ln x)+c₂sin(4ln x), option d. Option b describes the same solution family because 4ln(2x)=4ln x+4ln 2 is a constant phase shift.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{4i}}}={e}^{\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{4i}}}={e}^{-\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{4i}}+B{x}^{-\text{4i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 1
?

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+xy′+16y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡4x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡4x)
b
y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡2x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡2x)
c
y(x)=c1x+c24xln⁡x
d
y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=c14x2+c24x2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+x⋅λxλ−1+16xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+λxλ+16xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+16]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+16=0λ2+16=0λ2=−16.

Hence, the roots are λ=±4i.

Now, we note

x4i=eln⁡x4i=e4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x),x−4i=eln⁡x−4i=e−4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4iy(x)=A(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x))y(x)=(A+B)cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+i(A−B)sin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Finally, we can rewrite y(x) as y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+16y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+16{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+16 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{4i}}}={e}^{\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{4i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{4i}}}={e}^{-\text{4i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{4i}}+B{x}^{-\text{4i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+xy′+y=0,x>0.

a
 y(x)=c1x+c2x
b
 y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=c1x+c2xln⁡x
d
 y(x)=c1x2+c2x2
e
 y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡2x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡2x)
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^λ yields λ(λ−1)+λ+1=λ²+1=0, with roots ±i. Hence the general solution is c₁cos(ln x)+c₂sin(ln x), option b. Option e is equivalent because ln(2x)=ln x+ln 2 introduces a constant phase shift absorbed into the arbitrary coefficients.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{i}}+B{x}^{-\text{i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

after.html:
Question 2
?

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″+xy′+y=0,x>0.

a
 y(x)=c1x+c2x
b
 y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=c1x+c2xln⁡x
d
 y(x)=c1x2+c2x2
e
 y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡2x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡2x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+x⋅λxλ−1+xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+λxλ+xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+1]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+1=0λ2+1=0λ2=−1.

Hence, the roots are λ=±i.

Now, we note

xi=eln⁡xi=eiln⁡x=cos⁡(ln⁡x)+isin⁡(ln⁡x),x−i=eln⁡x−i=e−iln⁡x=cos⁡(ln⁡x)−isin⁡(ln⁡x).

Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=Axi+Bx−iy(x)=A(cos⁡(ln⁡x)+isin⁡(ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(ln⁡x)−isin⁡(ln⁡x))y(x)=(A+B)cos⁡(ln⁡x)+i(A−B)sin⁡(ln⁡x).

Finally, we can rewrite y(x) as y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms λ²+1=0, so λ=±i and option b is the general solution. Option e is mathematically equivalent: ln(2x)=ln x+ln 2, and the angle addition identities absorb this constant phase shift into the arbitrary coefficients, despite its displayed rejection.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{\text{i}}+B{x}^{-\text{i}} \\ y(x) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ y(x) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

y(t)=c1t7+c2t7ln⁡t
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡7t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡7t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡(t+7))+c2sin⁡(ln⁡(t+7))
d
y(t)=c1cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(7ln⁡t)

decision.explanation: Substituting y=t^λ gives λ(λ−1)+λ+7=λ²+7=0, whose roots are ±i√7. Therefore the general solution is c₁cos(√7 ln t)+c₂sin(√7 ln t), option d.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{7}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 3
?

Find the general solution to the equation t2y″+ty′+7y=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=c1t7+c2t7ln⁡t
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡7t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡7t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡(t+7))+c2sin⁡(ln⁡(t+7))
d
y(t)=c1cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(7ln⁡t)
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(7ln⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2+t⋅λtλ−1+7tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ+λtλ+7tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+7]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+7=0λ2+7=0λ2=−7.

Hence, the roots are λ=±7i.

Now, we note that t7i=eln⁡t7i=ei7ln⁡t=cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+isin⁡(7ln⁡t)t−7i=eln⁡t−7i=e−i7ln⁡t=cos⁡(7ln⁡t)−isin⁡(7ln⁡t).

Therefore, the general solution is y(t)=At7i+Bt−7iy(t)=A(cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+isin⁡(7ln⁡t))+B(cos⁡(7ln⁡t)−isin⁡(7ln⁡t))y(t)=(A+B)cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+i(A−B)sin⁡(7ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=c1cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(7ln⁡t),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-7.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{7}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{7}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{7}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{7}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Find the general solution to the equation 3t2y″+3ty′+18y=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=c1cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(6ln⁡t)
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡6t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡6t)
d
y(t)=c1cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(6ln⁡t)
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡(t+6))+c2sin⁡(ln⁡(t+6))
Submit

decision.explanation: Dividing by 3 gives t²y″+ty′+6y=0. Substituting y=t^λ yields λ²+6=0, so λ=±i√6. Thus the general solution is c₁cos(√6 ln t)+c₂sin(√6 ln t), option d.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
3{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+3t{y}^{′}+18y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 3\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18 & =0 \\ 3{\lambda }^{2}+18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Find the general solution to the equation 3t2y″+3ty′+18y=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=c1cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(6ln⁡t)
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡6t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡6t)
d
y(t)=c1cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(6ln⁡t)
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡(t+6))+c2sin⁡(ln⁡(t+6))
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

3t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2+3t⋅λtλ−1+18tλ=03λ(λ−1)tλ+3λtλ+18tλ=0tλ[3λ(λ−1)+3λ+18]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

3λ(λ−1)+3λ+18=03λ2+18=0λ2=−6.

Hence, the roots are λ=±6i.

Now, we note that t6i=eln⁡t6i=ei6ln⁡t=cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+isin⁡(6ln⁡t)t−6i=eln⁡t−6i=e−i6ln⁡t=cos⁡(6ln⁡t)−isin⁡(6ln⁡t).

Therefore, the general solution is y(t)=At6i+Bt−6iy(t)=A(cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+isin⁡(6ln⁡t))+B(cos⁡(6ln⁡t)−isin⁡(6ln⁡t))y(t)=(A+B)cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+i(A−B)sin⁡(6ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=c1cos⁡(6ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(6ln⁡t),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
3{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+3t{y}^{′}+18y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}3{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 3\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+18{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}3\lambda (\lambda -1)+3\lambda +18 & =0 \\ 3{\lambda }^{2}+18 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm \sqrt{6}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t) \\ {t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{\sqrt{6}\text{i}}+B{t}^{-\sqrt{6}\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{6}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

y(t)=c1cos⁡(9ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(9ln⁡t)
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡3t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡3t)
d

decision.explanation: Substituting y=t^λ gives λ(λ−1)+λ+9=λ²+9=0, with roots ±3i. Thus the general solution is c₁cos(3ln t)+c₂sin(3ln t), option b.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{3\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t), \\ {t}^{-3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-3\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{3\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 5
?

Find the general solution to the equation t2y″+ty′+9y=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=c1cos⁡(9ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(9ln⁡t)
b
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡3t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡3t)
d
y(t)=c1t3+c2t3ln⁡t
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡(t+9))+c2sin⁡(ln⁡(t+9))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2+t⋅λtλ−1+9tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ+λtλ+9tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+9]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+9=0λ2+9=0λ2=−9.

Hence, the roots are λ=±3i.

Now, we note that

t3i=eln⁡t3i=ei3ln⁡t=cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t),t−3i=eln⁡t−3i=e−i3ln⁡t=cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t).

Therefore, the general solution is y(t)=At3i+Bt−3iy(t)=A(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t))+B(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t))y(t)=(A+B)cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+i(A−B)sin⁡(3ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t),

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+9{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+9 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-9.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 3\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{3\text{i}}}={e}^{\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t), \\ {t}^{-3\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{t}^{-3\text{i}}}={e}^{-\text{i}3\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{3\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3\text{i}} \\ y(t) & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ y(t) & =(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

where  ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

decision.explanation: Substituting y=t^λ gives 2λ(λ−1)−2λ+6=0, or (λ−1)²+2=0. The roots are 1±i√2, so the general solution is t[c₁cos(√2 ln t)+c₂sin(√2 ln t)], option b.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+6y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-2t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+6{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-2\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+6{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +6] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +6 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1)-1+3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda -1 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{1+\sqrt{2}\text{i}} & =t{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{1-\sqrt{2}\text{i}} & =t{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{1+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}+B{t}^{1-\sqrt{2}\text{i}} \\  & =At(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+Bt(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B)t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as 

$$
y(t)=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 6
?

Find the general solution to the equation 2t2y″−2ty′+6y=0,t>0.

a
 y(t)=c1t+c2tln⁡t
b
y(t)=t(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=t2(c1cos⁡(ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡t+2)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡t+2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

2t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2−2t⋅λtλ−1+6tλ=02λ(λ−1)tλ−2λtλ+6tλ=0tλ[2λ(λ−1)−2λ+6]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

2λ(λ−1)−2λ+6=02λ2−4λ+6=02(λ2−2λ+3)=0λ2−2λ+3=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−2λ+3=0(λ2−2λ+1)−1+3=0(λ−1)2=−2λ−1=±2iλ=1±2i

Hence, the roots are λ=1±2i.

Now, we note that t1+2i=tei2ln⁡t=t(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t)),t1−2i=te−i2ln⁡t=t(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(t)=At1+2i+Bt1−2i=At(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t))+Bt(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t))=(A+B)tcos⁡(2ln⁡t)+i(A−B)tsin⁡(2ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=t(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t)), where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+6y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-2t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+6{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-2\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+6{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +6] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)-2\lambda +6 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +6 & =0 \\ 2({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +3 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1)-1+3 & =0 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =-2 \\ \lambda -1 & =\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1\pm \sqrt{2}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{1+\sqrt{2}\text{i}} & =t{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{1-\sqrt{2}\text{i}} & =t{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{1+\sqrt{2}\text{i}}+B{t}^{1-\sqrt{2}\text{i}} \\  & =At(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+Bt(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B)t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B)t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as 

$$
y(t)=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″−5xy′+12y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=x3(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
b
 y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
c
y(x)=c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=x2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
e
y(x)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡(x+3))+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡(x+3))

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^λ gives λ(λ−1)−5λ+12=λ²−6λ+12=0. Thus (λ−3)²=−3 and λ=3±i√3, yielding option a.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+12y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-5\lambda +12] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-5\lambda +12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +12 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+12 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =3\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3+\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ {x}^{3-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{3+\sqrt{3}\text{i}}+B{x}^{3-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} \\  & =A{x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B{x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B){x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B){x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={x}^{3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″−5xy′+12y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=x3(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
b
 y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
c
y(x)=c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=x2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x))
e
y(x)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡(x+3))+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡(x+3))
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2−5x⋅λxλ−1+12xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ−5λxλ+12xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)−5λ+12]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−5λ+12=0λ2−6λ+12=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−6λ+12=0(λ2−6λ+9)−9+12=0(λ−3)2=−3λ−3=±3iλ=3±3i

Hence, the roots are λ=3±3i.

Now, we note that x3+3i=x3ei3ln⁡x=x3(cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+isin⁡(3ln⁡x))x3−3i=x3e−i3ln⁡x=x3(cos⁡(3ln⁡x)−isin⁡(3ln⁡x)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is y(x)=Ax3+3i+Bx3−3i=Ax3(cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+isin⁡(3ln⁡x))+Bx3(cos⁡(3ln⁡x)−isin⁡(3ln⁡x))=(A+B)x3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+i(A−B)x3sin⁡(3ln⁡x).

Finally, we can rewrite y(x) as y(x)=x3(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x)) where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-5x{y}^{′}+12y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+12{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-5\lambda +12] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-5\lambda +12 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +12 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +12 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +9)-9+12 & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda -3 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =3\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =3\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3+\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\ {x}^{3-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={x}^{3}{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{3+\sqrt{3}\text{i}}+B{x}^{3-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} \\  & =A{x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B{x}^{3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B){x}^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B){x}^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={x}^{3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 8

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″−xy′+6y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x+1)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x−1)
b
y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x))
c
y(x)=c1e1+5x+c2xe1−5x
d
y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x))
e
y(x)=x2(c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x))
Submit

decision.explanation: Substituting y=x^λ gives λ(λ−1)−λ+6=λ²−2λ+6=0. Hence (λ−1)²=−5 and λ=1±i√5. The general solution is x[c₁cos(√5 ln x)+c₂sin(√5 ln x)], option b.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+6y=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +6] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =-5 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =-5 \\ \lambda -1 & =\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =1\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1+\sqrt{5}\text{i}} & =x{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)), \\ {x}^{1-\sqrt{5}\text{i}} & =x{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{1+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}+B{x}^{1-\sqrt{5}\text{i}} \\  & =Ax(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+Bx(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B)x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as 

$$
y(x)=x({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 8
?

Find the general solution to the equation x2y″−xy′+6y=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x+1)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x−1)
b
y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x))
c
y(x)=c1e1+5x+c2xe1−5x
d
y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x))
e
y(x)=x2(c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2−x⋅λxλ−1+6xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ−λxλ+6xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)−λ+6]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−λ+6=0λ2−2λ+6=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−2λ+1=−5(λ−1)2=−5λ−1=±5iλ=1±5i

Hence, the roots are λ=1±5i.

Now, we note that x1+5i=xei5ln⁡x=x(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+isin⁡(5ln⁡x)),x1−5i=xe−i5ln⁡x=x(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−isin⁡(5ln⁡x)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(x)=Ax1+5i+Bx1−5i=Ax(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+isin⁡(5ln⁡x))+Bx(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−isin⁡(5ln⁡x))=(A+B)xcos⁡(5ln⁡x)+i(A−B)xsin⁡(5ln⁡x).

Therefore, we can rewrite y(x) as

y(x)=x(c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x)), where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-x{y}^{′}+6y=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+6{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +6] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-\lambda +6 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +6 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +1 & =-5 \\ (\lambda -1)^{2} & =-5 \\ \lambda -1 & =\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =1\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =1\pm \sqrt{5}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{1+\sqrt{5}\text{i}} & =x{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)), \\ {x}^{1-\sqrt{5}\text{i}} & =x{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=x(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{1+\sqrt{5}\text{i}}+B{x}^{1-\sqrt{5}\text{i}} \\  & =Ax(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+Bx(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B)x\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)x\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as 

$$
y(x)=x({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

b

decision.explanation: Substituting y=t^λ gives λ(λ−1)−3λ+7=λ²−4λ+7=0. Thus (λ−2)²=−3, so λ=2±i√3. The general solution is t²[c₁cos(√3 ln t)+c₂sin(√3 ln t)], option a.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =-3 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}}+B{t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as 

$$
y(t)={t}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Question 9
?

Find the general solution to the equation t2y″−3ty′+7y=0,t>0.

a
y(t)=t2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
b
 y(t)=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=t2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)
e
y(t)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡(t+3))+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡(t+3))
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2−3t⋅λtλ−1+7tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ−3λtλ+7tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)−3λ+7]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−3λ+7=0λ2−4λ+7=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−4λ+4=−3(λ−2)2=−3λ−2=±3iλ=2±3i

Hence, the roots are λ=2±3i.

Now, we note that t2+3i=t2ei3ln⁡t=t2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t)),t2−3i=t2e−i3ln⁡t=t2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(t)=At2+3i+Bt2−3i=At2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t))+Bt2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t))=(A+B)t2cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+i(A−B)t2sin⁡(3ln⁡t).

Therefore, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=t2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms λ²−4λ+7=0, with roots 2±i√3. Therefore the general solution requires the factor t² and trigonometric arguments √3 ln t, exactly as in option a. Option b has the wrong power of t.

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-3t{y}^{′}+7y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =-3 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}}+B{t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as 

$$
y(t)={t}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

history.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-3t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+7{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +7 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +7 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4 & =-3 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-3 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =2\pm \sqrt{3}\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} & ={t}^{2}{e}^{-\text{i}\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{2+\sqrt{3}\text{i}}+B{t}^{2-\sqrt{3}\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as 

$$
y(t)={t}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2−3t⋅λtλ−1+7tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ−3λtλ+7tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)−3λ+7]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−3λ+7=0λ2−4λ+7=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−4λ+4=−3(λ−2)2=−3λ−2=±3iλ=2±3i

Hence, the roots are λ=2±3i.

Now, we note that t2+3i=t2ei3ln⁡t=t2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t)),t2−3i=t2e−i3ln⁡t=t2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(t)=At2+3i+Bt2−3i=At2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+isin⁡(3ln⁡t))+Bt2(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−isin⁡(3ln⁡t))=(A+B)t2cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+i(A−B)t2sin⁡(3ln⁡t).

Therefore, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=t2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Your Answer:
y(t)=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))

b
y(t)=t−3(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(2ln⁡3t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡3t)
d
y(t)=t3(c1cos⁡(ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡t))

decision.explanation: Substituting y=t^λ gives λ(λ−1)+7λ+13=λ²+6λ+13=0. Thus (λ+3)²=−4 and λ=−3±2i, yielding option b.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+7t{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-3\pm 2\text{i}.$

Note that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{-3+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{-3-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{-3+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={t}^{-3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

after.html:
Question 10
?

Find the general solution to the equation t2y″+7ty′+13y=0,t>0.

a
 y(t)=t−3(c1cos⁡(7ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(7ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=t−3(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=c1cos⁡(2ln⁡3t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡3t)
d
y(t)=t3(c1cos⁡(ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=t−2(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2+7t⋅λtλ−1+13tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ+7λtλ+13tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)+7λ+13]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+7λ+13=0λ2+6λ+13=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2+6λ+13=0(λ2+6λ+9)−9+13=0(λ+3)2=−4λ+3=±2iλ=−3±2i

Hence, the roots are λ=−3±2i.

Note that: t−3+2i=t−3ei2ln⁡t=t−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t)),t−3−2i=t−3e−i2ln⁡t=t−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t)).

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(t)=At−3+2i+Bt−3−2i=At−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t))+Bt−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t))=(A+B)t−3cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+i(A−B)t−3sin⁡(2ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=t−3(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t)) where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

content.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+7t{y}^{′}+13y=0,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}+7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }+7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+13{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+7\lambda +13 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +13 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda +9)-9+13 & =0 \\ (\lambda +3)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda +3 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-3\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-3\pm 2\text{i}.$

Note that:

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{-3+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{-3-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{-3}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{-3+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{-3-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{-3}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{-3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(t)$ as

$$
y(t)={t}^{-3}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

y(t)=At−3+2i+Bt−3−2i=At−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t))+Bt−3(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t))=(A+B)t−3cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+i(A−B)t−3sin⁡(2ln⁡t).

Finally, we can rewrite y(t) as

y(t)=t−3(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t)) where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

before.html:
Question 11
?

Given that the differential equation t2y″+ty′+2y=0 has the general solution y(t)=c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t), solve the initial value problem t2y″+ty′+2y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=1,t>0.

a
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
b
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t+2)
c
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡(t−2))
d
 y(t)=−12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
e
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since ln(1)=0, y(1)=0 gives c₁=0. Differentiating gives y′(t)=(√2/t)c₂cos(√2 ln t), so y′(1)=1 implies c₂=1/√2. Thus option e satisfies the equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{2}\,{t}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$

after.html:
Question 11
?

Given that the differential equation t2y″+ty′+2y=0 has the general solution y(t)=c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t), solve the initial value problem t2y″+ty′+2y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=1,t>0.

a
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
b
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t+2)
c
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡(t−2))
d
 y(t)=−12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
e
 y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(1)=0 into the general solution gives 0=c1.

  • To apply the condition y′(1)=1, we first differentiate y to get y′=2t−1(c2cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−c1sin⁡(2ln⁡t)).

Then, we substitute y′(1)=1 and c1=0 into the above gives 1=2c2c2=12.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(t)=12sin⁡(2ln⁡t).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+2y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =\sqrt{2}\,{t}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\sqrt{2}{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$

before.html:
Question 12
?

Given that the differential equation x2y″+xy′+y=0 has the general solution y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x), solve the initial value problem x2y″+xy′+y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=−5,x>0.

a
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡x)+5sin⁡(ln⁡x)
b
 y(x)=5cos⁡(2ln⁡x)+2sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡x)−5sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
 y(x)=cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
e
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡2x)−5sin⁡(ln⁡2x)
Submit

decision.explanation: Since ln(1)=0, y(1)=c₁=2. Differentiating gives y′(x)=[−c₁sin(ln x)+c₂cos(ln x)]/x, so y′(1)=c₂=−5. Therefore option c satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-5,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-5$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & ={c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

after.html:
Question 12
?

Given that the differential equation x2y″+xy′+y=0 has the general solution y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x), solve the initial value problem x2y″+xy′+y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=−5,x>0.

a
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡x)+5sin⁡(ln⁡x)
b
 y(x)=5cos⁡(2ln⁡x)+2sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡x)−5sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
 y(x)=cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
e
 y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡2x)−5sin⁡(ln⁡2x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(1)=2 into the general solution gives 2=c1.

  • To apply the condition y′(1)=−5, we first differentiate y to get y′=x−1(c2cos⁡(ln⁡x)−c1sin⁡(ln⁡x)). Then, we substitute y′(1)=−5 and c1=2 into the above gives −5=c2c2=−5.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=2cos⁡(ln⁡x)−5sin⁡(ln⁡x).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c₁=y(1)=2 and c₂=y′(1)=−5, giving option c. Its derivative is [−2sin(ln x)−5cos(ln x)]/x, which equals −5 at x=1. The deliberately submitted option d fails y(1)=2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-5,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-5,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & ={x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-5$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-5 & ={c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-5\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

before.html:
Question 13
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

2x2y″+2xy′+32y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=cos⁡(2ln⁡x)+sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
b
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)
c
y(x)=−3sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=−3cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
Submit

decision.explanation: Dividing by 2 gives x²y″+xy′+16y=0, with characteristic roots ±4i. Thus y=c₁cos(4ln x)+c₂sin(4ln x). The conditions y(1)=1 and y′(1)=0 give c₁=1 and 4c₂=0, so option b is the solution.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}+32y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+2x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+2\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+32 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4\text{i}}}={e}^{4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ {x}^{-4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-4\text{i}}}={e}^{-4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$
