after.html:
Question 13
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

2x2y″+2xy′+32y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=0,x>0.

a
y(x)=cos⁡(2ln⁡x)+sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
b
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)
c
y(x)=−3sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=−3cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

2x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+2x⋅λxλ−1+32xλ=02λ(λ−1)xλ+2λxλ+32xλ=0xλ[2λ(λ−1)+2λ+32]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

2λ(λ−1)+2λ+32=02λ2+32=0λ2=−16.

Hence, the roots are λ=±4i.

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4i.

Now, we note that

x4i=eln⁡x4i=e4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x−4i=eln⁡x−4i=e−4iln⁡x=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x).

Therefore,

y(x)=Ax4i+Bx−4i=A(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x))=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x),

where we have set c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=1 into the general solution gives

1=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=0. First, we differentiate y to find y′:

y′=4x−1(c2cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−c1sin⁡(4ln⁡x))

Substituting y′(1)=0 and c1=1 into the above gives

0=4c2c2=0.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
2{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+2x{y}^{′}+32y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+2x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ 2\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+2\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+32{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}2\lambda (\lambda -1)+2\lambda +32 & =0 \\ 2{\lambda }^{2}+32 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-16.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 4\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{4\text{i}}}={e}^{4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\ {x}^{-4\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-4\text{i}}}={e}^{-4\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-4\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =4{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

before.name: Question 14
before.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+9y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,y(1)=3,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$

before.html:
Question 14
?

Given that the differential equation x2y″+xy′+9y=0 has the general solution y(x)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x), solve the initial value problem x2y″+xy′+9y=0,y(1)=3,y′(1)=1,x>0.

a
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x+3)+13sin⁡(3ln⁡x+3)
b
 y(x)=cos⁡(3ln⁡x)−13sin⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=3cos⁡(ln⁡x)−13sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+sin⁡(3ln⁡x)
e
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+13sin⁡(3ln⁡x)
Submit

decision.explanation: At x=1, ln(1)=0, so y(1)=c₁=3. Differentiating gives y′(x)=3[c₂cos(3ln x)−c₁sin(3ln x)]/x. Thus y′(1)=3c₂=1, giving c₂=1/3 and option e.

y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,y(1)=3,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=3$ into the general solution gives

$$
3={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=3$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

Given that the differential equation x2y″+xy′+9y=0 has the general solution y(x)=c1cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡x), solve the initial value problem x2y″+xy′+9y=0,y(1)=3,y′(1)=1,x>0.

a
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x+3)+13sin⁡(3ln⁡x+3)
b
 y(x)=cos⁡(3ln⁡x)−13sin⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=3cos⁡(ln⁡x)−13sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+sin⁡(3ln⁡x)
e
 y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+13sin⁡(3ln⁡x)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(1)=3 into the general solution gives 3=c1.

  • To apply the condition y′(1)=1, we first differentiate y to get y′=3x−1(c2cos⁡(3ln⁡x)−c1sin⁡(3ln⁡x)). Then, we substitute y′(1)=1 and c1=3 into the above gives 1=3c2c2=13.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=3cos⁡(3ln⁡x)+13sin⁡(3ln⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+9y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+9y=0,\,y(1)=3,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=3$ into the general solution gives

$$
3={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =3{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ and ${c}_{1}=3$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is λ²+25=0, so y=c₁cos(5ln x)+c₂sin(5ln x). Since y(1)=0, c₁=0. Also y′(1)=5c₂=−1, giving c₂=−1/5. Thus option b satisfies the equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-1,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 5\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{5\text{i}}}={e}^{5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-5\text{i}}}={e}^{-5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-1$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =5{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

Question 15
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

x2y″+xy′+25y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=−1,x>0.

a
y(x)=cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+2sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
b
y(x)=−15sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
c
y(x)=2cos⁡(5ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=12cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−sin⁡(5ln⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+x⋅λxλ−1+25xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+λxλ+25xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+λ+25]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+λ+25=0λ2+25=0λ2=−25.

Hence, the roots are λ=±5i.

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

y(x)=Ax5i+Bx−5i.

Now, we note that

x5i=eln⁡x5i=e5iln⁡x=cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+isin⁡(5ln⁡x),x−5i=eln⁡x−5i=e−5iln⁡x=cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−isin⁡(5ln⁡x).

Therefore,

y(x)=Ax5i+Bx−5i=A(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+isin⁡(5ln⁡x))+B(cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−isin⁡(5ln⁡x))=c1cos⁡(5ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(5ln⁡x),

where we have set c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=0 into the general solution gives

0=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=−1. First, we differentiate y to find y′:

y′=5x−1(c2cos⁡(5ln⁡x)−c1sin⁡(5ln⁡x))

Substituting y′(1)=−1 and c1=0 into the above gives

−1=5c2c2=−15.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=−15sin⁡(5ln⁡x).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-1,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 5\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{5\text{i}}}={e}^{5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-5\text{i}}}={e}^{-5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-1$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =5{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

history.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+25{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+\lambda +25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+25 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2} & =-25.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =\pm 5\text{i}.$  

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
y(x)=A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}}.
$$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{5\text{i}}}={e}^{5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x), \\ {x}^{-5\text{i}} & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{-5\text{i}}}={e}^{-5\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{5\text{i}}+B{x}^{-5\text{i}} \\  & =A(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & ={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x),\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1.$ First, we differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-1$ and ${c}_{1}=0$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =5{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=-\frac{1}{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is λ(λ−1)−7λ+20=λ²−8λ+20=0, giving λ=4±2i. Thus y=t⁴[c₁cos(2ln t)+c₂sin(2ln t)]. The conditions imply c₁=0 and y′(1)=2c₂=2, so c₂=1. Therefore option b is the solution.

after.name: Question 16
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-7t{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16)-16+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -4 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =4\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =4\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ {t}^{4-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{4+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{4-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(t)$ as follows:

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=0$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2{c}_{2}{t}^{3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$

Question 16
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

t2y″−7ty′+20y=0,y(1)=0,y′(1)=2,t>0.

a
y(t)=−t2(5cos⁡(ln⁡t)+3sin⁡(ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=t4sin⁡(2ln⁡t)
c
y(t)=t4(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−3sin⁡(2ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=−5t2sin⁡(ln⁡t)
e
y(t)=−7t4cos⁡(2ln⁡t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=tλ. Differentiating y with respect to t gives

y′=λtλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)tλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

t2⋅λ(λ−1)tλ−2−7t⋅λtλ−1+20tλ=0λ(λ−1)tλ−7λtλ+20tλ=0tλ[λ(λ−1)−7λ+20]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)−7λ+20=0λ2−8λ+20=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2−8λ+20=0(λ2−8λ+16)−16+20=0(λ−4)2=−4λ−4=±2iλ=4±2i

Hence, the roots are λ=4±2i.

Now, we note that t4+2i=t4ei2ln⁡t=t4(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t))t4−2i=t4e−i2ln⁡t=t4(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t)).

Therefore, the general solution is

y(t)=At4+2i+Bt4−2i=At4(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+isin⁡(2ln⁡t))+Bt4(cos⁡(2ln⁡t)−isin⁡(2ln⁡t))=(A+B)t4cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+i(A−B)t4sin⁡(2ln⁡t).

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for y(t) as follows:

y(t)=t4(c1cos⁡(2ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(2ln⁡t))

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=0 into the general solution gives

0=c1.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-7t{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=2,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-7t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-7\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+20{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-7\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-8\lambda +16)-16+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda -4)^{2} & =-4 \\ \lambda -4 & =\pm 2\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =4\pm 2\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =4\pm 2\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{4+2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\ {t}^{4-2\text{i}} & ={t}^{4}{e}^{-\text{i}2\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{4+2\text{i}}+B{t}^{4-2\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{4}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{4}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(t)$ as follows:

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=0$ into the general solution gives

$$
0={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=0$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & =2{c}_{2}{t}^{3}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =2{c}_{2} \\ 1 & ={c}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={t}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$

Question 17
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem x2y″+5xy′+5y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=−2,x>0.

a
y(x)=x2(cos⁡(ln⁡x)−4sin⁡(ln⁡x))
b
 y(x)=x2cos⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=x2cos⁡(ln⁡x)+sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=cos⁡(ln⁡x)+2sin⁡(ln⁡x)x2
e
y(x)=cos⁡(ln⁡x)x2
Submit

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is λ(λ−1)+5λ+5=λ²+4λ+5=0, with roots −2±i. Thus y=x⁻²[c₁cos(ln x)+c₂sin(ln x)]. The initial conditions give c₁=1 and −2c₁+c₂=−2, so c₂=0. Therefore option e is the solution.

after.name: Question 17
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =-1 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-2+\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{-2-\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{-2+\text{i}}+B{x}^{-2-\text{i}} \\  & =A\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}+B\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=1$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{({c}_{2}-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-(1+2{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & ={c}_{2}-2 \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Question 17
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem x2y″+5xy′+5y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=−2,x>0.

a
y(x)=x2(cos⁡(ln⁡x)−4sin⁡(ln⁡x))
b
 y(x)=x2cos⁡(ln⁡x)
c
 y(x)=x2cos⁡(ln⁡x)+sin⁡(ln⁡x)
d
y(x)=cos⁡(ln⁡x)+2sin⁡(ln⁡x)x2
e
y(x)=cos⁡(ln⁡x)x2
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+5x⋅λxλ−1+5xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+5λxλ+5xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+5λ+5]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+5λ+5=0λ2+4λ+5=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2+4λ+4=−1(λ+2)2=−1λ+2=±i

Hence, the roots are λ=−2±i.

Now, we note that x−2+i=eiln⁡xx2=cos⁡(ln⁡x)+isin⁡(ln⁡x)x2x−2−i=e−iln⁡xx2=cos⁡(ln⁡x)−isin⁡(ln⁡x)x2.

Therefore, the general solution is y(x)=Ax−2+i+Bx−2−i=Acos⁡(ln⁡x)+isin⁡(ln⁡x)x2+Bcos⁡(ln⁡x)−isin⁡(ln⁡x)x2=(A+B)cos⁡(ln⁡x)+i(A−B)sin⁡(ln⁡x)x2.

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for y(x) as follows: y(x)=c1cos⁡(ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(ln⁡x)x2 where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=1 into the general solution gives 1=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=−2. First, we substitute c1=1 and differentiate y to find y′: y′(x)=(c2−2)cos⁡(ln⁡x)−(1+2c2)sin⁡(ln⁡x)x3

Substituting y′(1)=−2 into the above gives −2=c2−2c2=0.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=cos⁡(ln⁡x)x2.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms roots −2±i and y=x⁻²[c₁cos(ln x)+c₂sin(ln x)]. The initial conditions give c₁=1 and −2c₁+c₂=−2, hence c₂=0. Option e is correct; the deliberately submitted option b instead has y′(1)=2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4 & =-1 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-2+\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{-2-\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{-2+\text{i}}+B{x}^{-2-\text{i}} \\  & =A\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}+B\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=1$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =\frac{({c}_{2}-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-(1+2{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & ={c}_{2}-2 \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

before.html:
Question 18
?

Given that the differential equation 2t2y″−2ty′+20y=0 has the general solution y=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), solve the initial value problem 2t2y″−2ty′+20y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=−2,t>0.

a
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=3t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=1, y(1)=c₁=1. The product and chain rules give y′(1)=c₁+3c₂=−2, so c₂=−1. Therefore option c satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 18
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+20y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({c}_{1}+3{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+({c}_{2}-3{c}_{1})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =1+3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

after.html:
Question 18
?

Given that the differential equation 2t2y″−2ty′+20y=0 has the general solution y=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), solve the initial value problem 2t2y″−2ty′+20y=0,y(1)=1,y′(1)=−2,t>0.

a
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=3t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(1)=1 into the general solution gives 1=c1.

  • To apply the condition y′(1)=−2, we first differentiate y to get y′(x)=(c1+3c2)cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+(c2−3c1)sin⁡(3ln⁡t). Then, we substitute y′(1)=−2 and c1=1 into the above to get −2=1+3c2c2=−1.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(t)=t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t)).

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+20y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
2{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-2t{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({c}_{1}+3{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+({c}_{2}-3{c}_{1})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =1+3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

Question 19
?

Given that the differential equation t2y″−ty′+10y=0 has the general solution y=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), solve the initial value problem t2y″−ty′+10y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=−4,t>0.

a
y(t)=t(2cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−3sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=3t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=t(3cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
Submit

decision.explanation: At t=1, y(1)=c₁=2. Differentiating the general solution gives y′(1)=c₁+3c₂=−4, so c₂=−2. Thus option c satisfies the differential equation and both initial conditions.

after.name: Question 19
after.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-t{y}^{′}+10y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-t{y}^{′}+10y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-4,\,t>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-4,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({c}_{1}+3{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+({c}_{2}-3{c}_{1})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-4$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2+3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=2t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

Question 19
?

Given that the differential equation t2y″−ty′+10y=0 has the general solution y=t(c1cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+c2sin⁡(3ln⁡t)), solve the initial value problem t2y″−ty′+10y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=−4,t>0.

a
y(t)=t(2cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−3sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
b
y(t)=3t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
c
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
d
y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
e
y(t)=t(3cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−2sin⁡(3ln⁡t))
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We find the constants c1 and c2 using the initial conditions.

  • Substituting y(1)=2 into the general solution gives 2=c1.

  • To apply the condition y′(1)=−4, we first differentiate y to get y′(x)=(c1+3c2)cos⁡(3ln⁡t)+(c2−3c1)sin⁡(3ln⁡t). Then, we substitute y′(1)=−4 and c1=2 into the above to get −4=2+3c2c2=−2.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(t)=2t(cos⁡(3ln⁡t)−sin⁡(3ln⁡t)).

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c₁=2 and c₂=−2 because y(1)=c₁ and y′(1)=c₁+3c₂=−4. Thus option c satisfies the equation and both initial conditions. The deliberately submitted option b gives y(1)=3 instead of 2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-t{y}^{′}+10y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=t({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-t{y}^{′}+10y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-4,\,t>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-4,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =({c}_{1}+3{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+({c}_{2}-3{c}_{1})\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-4$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =2+3{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=2t(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

decision.explanation: The characteristic equation is λ(λ−1)+5λ+20=λ²+4λ+20=0, with roots −2±4i. Thus y=x⁻²[c₁cos(4ln x)+c₂sin(4ln x)]. The initial conditions give c₁=2 and −2c₁+4c₂=−4, hence c₂=0. Therefore option a is the solution.

after.name: Question 20
after.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-4,\,x>0.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +4)-4+20 & =0 \\ (\lambda +2)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda +2 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =-2\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =-2\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{-2+4\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{-2-4\text{i}} & =\frac{{e}^{-\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{{x}^{2}}=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{-2+4\text{i}}+B{x}^{-2-4\text{i}} \\  & =A\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}+B\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(A+B)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(x)=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-4.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=2$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-\frac{2[(4+{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2-2{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)]}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=-4$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-4 & =-2[2-2{c}_{2}] \\ -4 & =-4+4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
$$

Question 20
?

Find the solution to the initial value problem

x2y″+5xy′+20y=0,y(1)=2,y′(1)=−4,x>0.

a
y(x)=2cos⁡(4ln⁡x)x2
b
y(x)=xcos⁡(4ln⁡x)
c
y(x)=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+3sin⁡(4ln⁡x)x
d
y(x)=x2(cos⁡(2ln⁡x)−2sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
e
y(x)=−x3sin⁡(2ln⁡x)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form y=xλ. Differentiating y with respect to x gives

y′=λxλ−1,y″=λ(λ−1)xλ−2.

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

x2⋅λ(λ−1)xλ−2+5x⋅λxλ−1+20xλ=0λ(λ−1)xλ+5λxλ+20xλ=0xλ[λ(λ−1)+5λ+20]=0.

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

λ(λ−1)+5λ+20=0λ2+4λ+20=0.

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

λ2+4λ+20=0(λ2+4λ+4)−4+20=0(λ+2)2=−16λ+2=±4iλ=−2±4i

Hence, the roots are λ=−2±4i.

Now, we note that x−2+4i=ei4ln⁡xx2=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2x−2−4i=e−i4ln⁡xx2=cos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2.

Therefore, the general solution is

y(x)=Ax−2+4i+Bx−2−4i=Acos⁡(4ln⁡x)+isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2+Bcos⁡(4ln⁡x)−isin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2=(A+B)cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+i(A−B)sin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2.

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for y(x) as follows:

y(x)=c1cos⁡(4ln⁡x)+c2sin⁡(4ln⁡x)x2

where c1=A+B and c2=i(A−B).

Now let's find the constants c1 and c2.

Substituting y(1)=2 into the general solution gives

2=c1.

We now need to apply the condition y′(1)=−4. First, we substitute c1=2 and differentiate y to find y′:

y′(x)=−2[(4+c2)sin⁡(4ln⁡x)+(2−2c2)cos⁡(4ln⁡x)]x3

Substituting y′(1)=−4 into the above gives −4=−2[2−2c2]−4=−4+4c2c2=0.

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is y(x)=2cos⁡(4ln⁡x)x2.

content.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
content.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+5x{y}^{′}+20y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-4,\,x>0.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}+5x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }+5\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+20{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)+5\lambda +20 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +20 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}-4 & =-2[2-2{c}_{2}] \\ -4 & =-4+4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y(x)=\frac{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{{x}^{2}}.
